Israeli soldiers deployed in Tulkarm refugee camp in the occupied West Bank look on as displaced Palestinians granted temporary permits retrieve belongings from their destroyed or heavily damaged homes on June 21, 2026. Photo by Aseel Mfarajeh.
JENIN, Occupied West Bank--It took Omar Qalib more than a decade to finish his family's three-story house in Jouret al-Dahab, a neighborhood in the heart of the Jenin refugee camp. A construction worker, he built it himself, brick by brick. But it was worth it, he thought. The property fell within Area A, a zone within the occupied West Bank where the Palestinian Authority nominally controls both civil and security affairs.
But in January 2025, Qalib was forced from his home, along with tens of thousands of other Palestinians, as Israel launched a large-scale military operation dubbed "Iron Wall" targeting refugee camps in Jenin, Tulkarm, and Nur Shams. More than 30,000 Palestinians were forced from their homes over the ensuing months, in the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank in a single operation since the 1967 war.
After invading and occupying the camps in February 2025, the Israeli military campaign flattened entire neighborhoods, turning them into wastelands. Where narrow alleys once ran between tall buildings so close they blocked the light, wide dirt roads now cut through the heart of the camps, carved out by Israeli military bulldozers.
As part of the campaign, the camps have been cordoned off. Just to see what's left of his home, Qalib needs a permit from the Israeli military. Few Palestinians are able to obtain them. And the permits only grant one-time, temporary access. Two weeks ago, Qalib was one of the lucky few who obtained a permit to visit his destroyed home.
"The house is gone," said Qalib "My house and my son's house. A whole life of work, gone."
Qalib, 56, now shares two rooms with his wife, two adult sons and their families, packed together in a dormitory connected to the Arab American university in the city of Jenin. "I had a whole family in that house," he said. "Now we are all in two rooms waiting for something we don't know when will end."
Every morning Qalib heads out looking for work as a day laborer, the principal breadwinner responsible for rent, food, electricity, water, and transportation costs for an entire household. Those costs have nearly doubled since they were displaced.
Both of Qalib's sons were shot by Israeli soldiers during the military invasion of the camp. One was left half paralyzed, with damage to his kidney, spleen, and lung, and is unable to work. His other son recovered from his injuries and is able to physically work though he has been able to find a job since they left their home, nearly a year and a half ago.
Recently, some Palestinians have been granted limited access to enter their old neighborhoods, mainly to scavenge in their destroyed or heavily damaged homes for items they left behind. What they described to Drop Site are neighborhoods made unrecognizable: men who spent their lives in these alleys wander in the middle of emptied out dirt roads, looking for a mosque that used to mark the turn, the building that used to anchor their route. The landmarks are gone. Some cannot even locate where their own homes once stood.
## **The First Permanent Israeli Military Base in Area A Since Oslo**
Alongside the large-scale destruction, the Israeli military is engaged in unprecedented construction. In May, the commander of Israel's Central Command signed an order to seize land in the city of Jenin, near the Jenin refugee camp, and construct a permanent military base, according to documents first [revealed](https://substack.com/redirect/8286d333-2a41-4eeb-980b-6de8ad2ef7b2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) by Haaretz. It marked the first time since the Oslo Accords in 1993 that the Israeli military has built a permanent post in Area A.
While the Israeli military has staged regular incursions into cities and towns in Area A for years, despite it technically being under Palestinian civil and security control, the establishment of a permanent Israeli military base represents a major shift. "The Area A designation was the foundational pillar of the concept of Palestinian self-governance," said Ibrahim Abras, a political analyst and academic. "A permanent military base inside these areas signals a shift in the nature of Israeli control, a gradual transition from managing the conflict through temporary incursions to imposing a long-term field presence that raises serious questions about the future legal and political status of these areas."
Putting a base in Jenin is "a mechanism for reshaping control over the land," said Ismat Mansour, a specialist in Israeli affairs. "A permanent base near Jenin gives Israel far greater leverage over the security and political landscape of the entire region."
Meanwhile, tens of thousands of Palestinians in the West Bank remain displaced from their homes, with no legal justification offered for blocking their return, according to [ACRI](https://substack.com/redirect/95d8cecf-269f-4793-9dee-90ff00b3f267?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), the Association for Civil Rights in Israel, which has described the situation as a systematic violation of the rights of an entire displaced population.
In late March, the Israeli security cabinet secretly [approved](https://substack.com/redirect/4d342dd4-c8ac-40b3-ba28-73892d6d7852?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) 34 settlements across the West Bank, including six of them that form a ring around Jenin. It marked the largest number of settlements and outposts approved by any Israeli government at one time.
"Many of the current settlements began as military positions or outposts before being converted into permanent civilian communities," said Khalil Tufakji, a settlements expert who has spent decades mapping the relationship between military infrastructure and settlement expansion.
The pattern, said Tufakji, is not new. "Reactivating evacuated outposts in the northern West Bank simultaneously with a permanent military base demands a wider reading about the future of the entire area."
The establishment and fortification of new Israeli settlements comes in parallel with the all but total restriction of permits for Palestinians to return to their homes. To enter a refugee camp a Palestinian was born in, grew up in, and subsequently displaced from, now requires Israeli military authorization. Palestinians who have managed to obtain a permit describe it as a one-time authorization that comes with no guarantee it will be granted again. The displacement has effectively become permanent.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/9ead3bed-93a7-4fdc-84e4-d3da93d48d96?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Israeli soldiers deployed in Tulkarm refugee camp in the occupied West Bank look on as displaced Palestinians granted temporary permits retrieve belongings from their destroyed or heavily damaged homes on June 21, 2026. Photo by Aseel Mfarajeh.
## **" When will we go back to our house?"**
Um Faris, 42, left Nur Shams camp in January 2025 with her five children, each carrying a piece of home in their hands.
Faris, 17, carried a small bag with the family's documents. His mother warned him not to lose it no matter what. The younger children each held onto something too: Ahmed, 14, keeps photos of the camp on his phone and spends hours looking at them. Layan, 8, brought a small cloth doll, the last piece of her old room. She goes to sleep every night holding it.
They left a big house with a backyard and now live in a small rented apartment with thin walls on the outskirts of Tulkarm. Before being displaced, her husband worked in construction. The road closures and movement restrictions ended that. Faris was forced to drop out of school to find work; he has stopped talking about finishing school and going to university. His younger siblings also eventually dropped out because they were unable to attend classes as a result of the severe restrictions on movement imposed by the Israeli army.
Um Faris has documents proving ownership of her home. But she does not have the permit to enter the area where it once stood. She's not sure what is even left of it. Every morning, her youngest child asks the same question: "When will we go back to our house?"
In Fahma, south of Jenin, 35-year-old Ahmed lives in a rented house with his family. He declined to give his last name for fear of Israeli retribution. Six of them share just two rooms, a space half the size of the home they left in the Jenin camp. The family shop that provided part of their household income is gone. Lately rents have been rising, and humanitarian assistance is being reduced. With no stable income, covering rent, food, and other household expenses has become a daily struggle.
Ahmed keeps the key to his old house in his pocket, hoping to return. On one of the rare occasions when he was briefly granted access, Ahmed walked through the alleys he grew up in.
Or, he tried to. "I thought I knew every stone," he said. "But I felt like a stranger. The streets I had memorized were gone. Buildings that had been fixed points in my memory had disappeared. Entire neighborhoods looked like they had been erased."
"The continued prevention of thousands of Palestinians from returning to their camps for months creates a new reality on the ground," said Ashraf al-Akka, a political analyst. "The social and economic fabric begins to break down gradually while physical changes inside the emptied areas continue. The prolonged displacement cannot be separated from broader Israeli policies aimed at reshaping Palestinian geography in the West Bank."
Worse yet, the periodic orders forcing displacement show no signs of stopping. In Qalandia and other camps across the West Bank, multiple residents told Drop Site that Israeli soldiers used loudspeakers to blare out a chilling warning during raids: "Prepare yourselves. What happened in Jenin and Tulkarm will happen to you."

Please consider becoming a paid subscriber or making a . | | ---|---|--- Israeli soldiers deployed in Tulkarm refugee camp in the occupied West Bank look on as displaced Palestinians granted temporary permits retrieve belongings from their destroyed or heavily damaged homes on June 21, 2026. Photo by Aseel Mfarajeh. JENIN, Occupied West Bank--It took Omar Qalib more than a decade to finish his family's three-story house in Jouret al-Dahab, a neighborhood in the heart of the Jenin refugee camp. A construction worker, he built it himself, brick by brick. But it was worth it, he thought. The property fell within Area A, a zone within the occupied West Bank where the Palestinian Authority nominally controls both civil and security affairs. But in January 2025, Qalib was forced from his home, along with tens of thousands of other Palestinians, as Israel launched a large-scale military operation dubbed "Iron Wall" targeting refugee camps in Jenin, Tulkarm, and Nur Shams. More than 30,000 Palestinians were forced from their homes over the ensuing months, in the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank in a single operation since the 1967 war. After invading and occupying the camps in February 2025, the Israeli military campaign flattened entire neighborhoods, turning them into wastelands. Where narrow alleys once ran between tall buildings so close they blocked the light, wide dirt roads now cut through the heart of the camps, carved out by Israeli military bulldozers. As part of the campaign, the camps have been cordoned off. Just to see what's left of his home, Qalib needs a permit from the Israeli military. Few Palestinians are able to obtain them. And the permits only grant one-time, temporary access. Two weeks ago, Qalib was one of the lucky few who obtained a permit to visit his destroyed home. "The house is gone," said Qalib "My house and my son's house. A whole life of work, gone." Qalib, 56, now shares two rooms with his wife, two adult sons and their families, packed together in a dormitory connected to the Arab American university in the city of Jenin. "I had a whole family in that house," he said. "Now we are all in two rooms waiting for something we don't know when will end." Every morning Qalib heads out looking for work as a day laborer, the principal breadwinner responsible for rent, food, electricity, water, and transportation costs for an entire household. Those costs have nearly doubled since they were displaced. Both of Qalib's sons were shot by Israeli soldiers during the military invasion of the camp. One was left half paralyzed, with damage to his kidney, spleen, and lung, and is unable to work. His other son recovered from his injuries and is able to physically work though he has been able to find a job since they left their home, nearly a year and a half ago. Recently, some Palestinians have been granted limited access to enter their old neighborhoods, mainly to scavenge in their destroyed or heavily damaged homes for items they left behind. What they described to Drop Site are neighborhoods made unrecognizable: men who spent their lives in these alleys wander in the middle of emptied out dirt roads, looking for a mosque that used to mark the turn, the building that used to anchor their route. The landmarks are gone. Some cannot even locate where their own homes once stood. The First Permanent Israeli Military Base in Area A Since Oslo Alongside the large-scale destruction, the Israeli military is engaged in unprecedented construction. In May, the commander of Israel's Central Command signed an order to seize land in the city of Jenin, near the Jenin refugee camp, and construct a permanent military base, according to documents first by Haaretz. It marked the first time since the Oslo Accords in 1993 that the Israeli military has built a permanent post in Area A. While the Israeli military has staged regular incursions into cities and towns in Area A for years, despite it technically being under Palestinian civil and security control, the establishment of a permanent Israeli military base represents a major shift. "The Area A designation was the foundational pillar of the concept of Palestinian self-governance," said Ibrahim Abras, a political analyst and academic. "A permanent military base inside these areas signals a shift in the nature of Israeli control, a gradual transition from managing the conflict through temporary incursions to imposing a long-term field presence that raises serious questions about the future legal and political status of these areas." Putting a base in Jenin is "a mechanism for reshaping control over the land," said Ismat Mansour, a specialist in Israeli affairs. "A permanent base near Jenin gives Israel far greater leverage over the security and political landscape of the entire region." Meanwhile, tens of thousands of Palestinians in the West Bank remain displaced from their homes, with no legal justification offered for blocking their return, according to , the Association for Civil Rights in Israel, which has described the situation as a systematic violation of the rights of an entire displaced population. In late March, the Israeli security cabinet secretly 34 settlements across the West Bank, including six of them that form a ring around Jenin. It marked the largest number of settlements and outposts approved by any Israeli government at one time. "Many of the current settlements began as military positions or outposts before being converted into permanent civilian communities," said Khalil Tufakji, a settlements expert who has spent decades mapping the relationship between military infrastructure and settlement expansion. The pattern, said Tufakji, is not new. "Reactivating evacuated outposts in the northern West Bank simultaneously with a permanent military base demands a wider reading about the future of the entire area." The establishment and fortification of new Israeli settlements comes in parallel with the all but total restriction of permits for Palestinians to return to their homes. To enter a refugee camp a Palestinian was born in, grew up in, and subsequently displaced from, now requires Israeli military authorization. Palestinians who have managed to obtain a permit describe it as a one-time authorization that comes with no guarantee it will be granted again. The displacement has effectively become permanent. | | ---|---|--- Israeli soldiers deployed in Tulkarm refugee camp in the occupied West Bank look on as displaced Palestinians granted temporary permits retrieve belongings from their destroyed or heavily damaged homes on June 21, 2026. Photo by Aseel Mfarajeh. " When will we go back to our house?" Um Faris, 42, left Nur Shams camp in January 2025 with her five children, each carrying a piece of home in their hands. Faris, 17, carried a small bag with the family's documents. His mother warned him not to lose it no matter what. The younger children each held onto something too: Ahmed, 14, keeps photos of the camp on his phone and spends hours looking at them. Layan, 8, brought a small cloth doll, the last piece of her old room. She goes to sleep every night holding it. They left a big house with a backyard and now live in a small rented apartment with thin walls on the outskirts of Tulkarm. Before being displaced, her husband worked in construction. The road closures and movement restrictions ended that. Faris was forced to drop out of school to find work; he has stopped talking about finishing school and going to university. His younger siblings also eventually dropped out because they were unable to attend classes as a result of the severe restrictions on movement imposed by the Israeli army. Um Faris has documents proving ownership of her home. But she does not have the permit to enter the area where it once stood. She's not sure what is even left of it. Every morning, her youngest child asks the same question: "When will we go back to our house?" In Fahma, south of Jenin, 35-year-old Ahmed lives in a rented house with his family. He declined to give his last name for fear of Israeli retribution. Six of them share just two rooms, a space half the size of the home they left in the Jenin camp. The family shop that provided part of their household income is gone. Lately rents have been rising, and humanitarian assistance is being reduced. With no stable income, covering rent, food, and other household expenses has become a daily struggle. Ahmed keeps the key to his old house in his pocket, hoping to return. On one of the rare occasions when he was briefly granted access, Ahmed walked through the alleys he grew up in. Or, he tried to. "I thought I knew every stone," he said. "But I felt like a stranger. The streets I had memorized were gone. Buildings that had been fixed points in my memory had disappeared. Entire neighborhoods looked like they had been erased." "The continued prevention of thousands of Palestinians from returning to their camps for months creates a new reality on the ground," said Ashraf al-Akka, a political analyst. "The social and economic fabric begins to break down gradually while physical changes inside the emptied areas continue. The prolonged displacement cannot be separated from broader Israeli policies aimed at reshaping Palestinian geography in the West Bank." Worse yet, the periodic orders forcing displacement show no signs of stopping. In Qalandia and other camps across the West Bank, multiple residents told Drop Site that Israeli soldiers used loudspeakers to blare out a chilling warning during raids: "Prepare yourselves. What happened in Jenin and Tulkarm will happen to you." This story was reported and produced in collaboration with. | A guest post by| field journalist interested in human interest stories. ## Bitcoin Was the Prototype
Say what you want about Bitcoin — it proved something the experts swore was impossible. It proved that millions of people want a way to store wealth that no government can print, freeze, or inflate away. That idea was radical in 2009. Today it's a trillion-dollar fact. But here's what the true believers don't like to admit: Bitcoin got the _idea_ right and the _backing_ wrong. It's backed by nothing but belief. It can lose a third of its value in a month. And it consumes as much electricity as a small country just to keep the lights on. It was the prototype. A brilliant, world-changing prototype — but a prototype all the same. So here's the question worth sitting with: what happens when someone takes everything Bitcoin got right — the digital freedom, the scarcity, the independence from any government — and fixes the one thing it got wrong, by backing it with real, verified gold? You get the finished version. And it starts trading on Kraken on **July 8**. And to be clear: this isn't another speculative crypto, and it isn't paper gold. It's backed by real, certified, in-ground gold — the gold stays right where it is, and the value trades. I'm not going to unpack the whole thing in an email. But I've been watching it closely, it's cleared one of the toughest exchanges in the world, and I put together the full briefing on what it is. [**See the finished version →**](https://link.email.america1stwarroom.com/click/e16793186/VaHR0cHM6Ly9zZWN1cmUyLndlYWx0aGRhaWx5LmNvbS9vL29wLzExNTgwNDM/SZW1haWxfYW1lcmljYU9ORXN0d2Fycm9vbV9jb20yNjA2MzA/LbmNsTjdvSXk4ag/gakQ2vA/sfia7d30c79) Get to the good, green grass first... **Brian Hicks, The Prophet of Profit**
President & Founder, Angel Publishing **P.S.** There's an estimated **$5 trillion** in verified gold sitting in the ground right now — real, proven, and completely frozen out of the digital economy. The thing launching July 8 is the first attempt to change that. [Here's how it works.](https://link.email.america1stwarroom.com/click/e16793186/VaHR0cHM6Ly9zZWN1cmUyLndlYWx0aGRhaWx5LmNvbS9vL29wLzExNTgwNDM/SZW1haWxfYW1lcmljYU9ORXN0d2Fycm9vbV9jb20yNjA2MzA/LbmNsTjdvSXk4ag/gakQ2vA/sfia7d30c79)

body:
We’re just hours away from our end-of-quarter deadline, and we’re hoping to hit our fundraising targets before then.
#
Can we be real with you for a moment?
We understand that a constant stream of emails asking for a contribution can sometimes get on your nerves. That’s okay. Real people wrote this email, we get them as well. We understand how people can get frustrated. _But let us explain why this is vital._
When we’re asking for your support, we don’t expect every person to give. But we ask because we know that when you can support the cause, you will. That’s how this transformative movement works. **It’s a whole lot of people doing their part to make something great.**
[ We’re just hours away from our end-of-quarter deadline, and we’re hoping to hit our fundraising targets before then. The only way we can is through the support of small-dollar donors chipping in whatever they can. If you can, will you make a $3 contribution — or $5, or anything you can — right now? It’ll go a long way.](https://act.ocasiocortez.com/go/14659?c0=aoc-email-20260630.CD1idd&refcode=em20260630-11840-P_FND_EGR_GRM&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=3&akid=11840%2E2526796%2EsPtOiK)

_A quick note before we start: this piece is about the civilian AI economy -- the financial structure behind chatbots, cloud computing, and the trillions of dollars chasing all of it. I have a separate, much harder piece coming on the military applications of AI, and that one does not give any benefit of the doubt. This one is about your job, your pension, and your power bill._
* * *
In 2024, a Swedish fintech company called Klarna built an AI customer-service assistant with OpenAI for somewhere around $2 to $3 million.
In its first month alone, it handled work equivalent to roughly 700 full-time agents. Klarna projected the assistant would add about $40 million to company profit that year. Run the ratio: $40 million in value, generated by avoiding the need for about 700 workers, off a $2-to-$3-million build. That's the spreadsheet every CFO in the country is staring at right now. If AI deployment works like that, it pays for itself dozens of times over in a single year.
That spreadsheet is the reason Nvidia is now worth more than $5 trillion. It's the reason seven tech stocks make up roughly a third of the entire S&P 500. It's the reason your pension fund, your 401(k), your state retirement system quietly became a leveraged bet on whether artificial intelligence delivers on promises it hasn't fully kept yet -- promises that would gut the economy as we've known it.
And nobody asked you.
Nobody asked you when Nvidia became worth more than any other company on Earth. Nobody asked you when your retirement savings became collateral for a bet you never consented to. Nobody asked you when the people selling you the future started needing you to believe in it more than they needed the technology to actually work.
You didn't get a vote. You got a balance statement.
And if some part of you has felt, these past couple of years, like something about the AI story doesn't quite add up -- like the hype is a half-step ahead of the actual product, like the people selling you the future have a few too many reasons to need you to believe them -- trust that feeling. You're not behind. You're paying attention.
Here's what's actually going on.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/67af5e09-d10b-47d0-8d60-413c36853b0c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* * *
## The Story We're Being Sold
The pitch is simple: artificial intelligence is the next industrial revolution. It will supercharge productivity, write your code, draft your emails, and eventually run a meaningful share of the economy with less human labor than we've ever needed before.
Some of that is real. I use AI tools myself, for research, and they're genuinely useful -- they kill busywork, they help me think through strategy, they help me make the most of every minute of time. This isn't an anti-technology piece.
But "useful" and "worth what Wall Street has bet on it" are two different questions. The gap between them is where the danger lives.
* * *
## Follow the Money
As of this week, Nvidia is worth more than $5 trillion. Microsoft is sitting around $2.7 trillion. Oracle, even after a rough June, is still worth roughly half a trillion. Add in Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Tesla, and those seven companies -- the "Magnificent Seven" -- make up roughly a third of the entire S&P 500.
That matters because, unless you've found some way to opt out of American capitalism's only real retirement system, you almost certainly own a slice of all of them. Index funds. Target-date funds. The teachers' pension. The firefighters' fund. The state employees' retirement system.
They all hold the S&P 500 heavily, as what's assumed to be a _safe, diversified, averaged holding_ that doesn't rely on any individual industry... -- but the S&P 500 is now, by design, a **concentrated bet on a handful of AI companies** , whether you chose that exposure or not.
According to a Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis analysis, AI-related investment -- chips, software, data centers, research and development -- accounted for roughly 39% of all U.S. economic growth in the first three quarters of 2025. Strip that spending out, and the "strong economy" DC keeps congratulating itself on mostly disappears.
**We are not in an AI-adjacent economy. We are in an AI-dependent one.**
And here's the part that should make us nervous: behind all those trillions in market cap is a question nobody in power wants to answer:
_How much of that "demand" is real customers buying a real product, and how much of it is a handful of companies financing each other in a loop?_
* * *
## The Circular Economy Machine
In March, OpenAI closed a $122 billion funding round at a valuation north of $850 billion. The headline made it sound like a wall of investor cash. Look closer and the structure tells a different story.
Nvidia's $30 billion of that round is largely compute credits, not cash -- money that flows back to Nvidia as OpenAI buys Nvidia's chips. Amazon put in $50 billion, but $35 billion of it is contingent on OpenAI either going public or hitting an artificial-general-intelligence milestone by year's end, meaning the actual committed cash on day one was a fraction of the headline number. SoftBank's $30 billion arrives in quarterly installments tied to OpenAI hitting its own targets along the way.
Meanwhile, Oracle has taken on a roughly $300 billion contractual obligation to supply OpenAI with computing capacity through 2032 -- financed through aggressive borrowing, against a balance sheet that just posted negative free cash flow of nearly $24 billion. Nvidia invests in OpenAI. OpenAI spends that money on Nvidia chips and Oracle compute. Oracle borrows billions to build the data centers OpenAI needs, betting OpenAI's future revenue covers the debt. Around and around it goes.
None of this is illegal. None of it is necessarily fraud in the technical sense -- whether it's fraud in the moral sense, or monopoly, or simply an absolutely terrible idea, is a different question.
When the chipmaker is also the investor, and the customer is also the landlord, and the financing itself is generating the "demand" rather than the other way around, you have to ask how much of this economy would still exist if the money stopped flowing.
Now return to that Klarna spreadsheet, because it explains everything that comes next.
* * *
## What "Replacing One Job" Is Actually Worth
Here's a question worth answering plainly: is there an actual ratio connecting "one job gone" to "one dollar in AI revenue"? Nobody publishes an official industry-wide formula. But there is a real mechanism underneath it, and it isn't complicated once you see it laid bare.
A company buys an AI tool for one reason: because the tool costs less than the human labor it lets the company avoid hiring or stop paying for. That's the entire business case, underneath a hundred different slide decks.
Klarna's math was clean on day one. But by 2025, Klarna was quietly rehiring humans, because the AI couldn't reliably handle complex disputes, fraud claims, or anything requiring real judgment -- the harder, messier third of the actual job. The ratio that looked so beautiful on the spreadsheet fell apart the moment the work got complicated.
That's the entire AI economy, in miniature. Multiply Klarna's story across every customer-service floor, every law firm, every hospital back office, every accounting department in America, and you get the real shape of the problem: the ratio works beautifully on the routine, repetitive slice of almost any job, and breaks down on the skilled, judgment-heavy slice that's usually most of what the job actually is.
Every dollar of revenue flowing to Nvidia, Microsoft, and Oracle ultimately depends on enough companies finding that math attractive across enough of the workforce to add up to trillions of dollars in sustained spending.
So far, the receipts say it adds up on the easy third. The debt was priced as if it adds up on the whole job.
* * *
## The Catch-22
Now here's where it gets fatal.
JPMorgan currently projects $5.5 trillion in global AI infrastructure spending by 2030, with roughly $4.1 trillion of it financed through debt, not cash. More than $300 billion in AI and data-center bonds have already been issued in 2026 alone.
Let's take a moment to get exquisitely clear about what "the debt has to be serviced" actually means, because this is the piece that explains everything else in this story.
When a company borrows money by selling a bond, it owes two separate things. The **principal** is the original amount borrowed. The **interest** is rent, charged every single year, just for the privilege of having borrowed the money at all. You can pay only the interest for years and never touch the principal -- the same way you can pay the minimum on a credit card forever without the balance ever shrinking. **But skip an interest payment, even once, and you 're in default.** The lender doesn't care how brilliant your business plan is. They want their check, in full, on the date printed on the bond.
Now scale that up to AI-industry size. Some of the roughly $4.1 trillion in projected debt is high-grade, pricing somewhere around 5 to 6 percent interest. A growing share is riskier, junk-rated data-center debt, which has been pricing at 7 to 9 percent, with at least one widely reported deal carrying a 12.5 percent coupon.
Even using a conservative blended estimate of 6 to 8 percent, the interest alone on $4.1 trillion comes out to somewhere between roughly $245 billion and $330 billion. Every single year. For as long as that debt is outstanding -- _before a single dollar of the original $4.1 trillion gets paid back._
Sit with that number. **Two hundred and forty-five to three hundred and thirty billion dollars, every year, just to stay current on interest** -- more than the entire annual economic output of most countries on the planet, and that's before the principal is touched at all.
That money has to come from somewhere real: customers paying for AI products at a scale that generates that much actual cash flow, growing every year fast enough to keep pace as more debt gets issued. And the only proven way AI generates that kind of return right now -- per the Klarna math above -- is by **displacing** labor costs at scale. Not gently assisting. _**Displacing**_.
If that doesn't scale fast enough across enough of the economy, the cash flow doesn't show up... -- and the interest payment is still due on the date printed on the bond, regardless of how the technology is actually performing in the real world that quarter.
**This is the fundamental, desperate engine behind the hype.** It is not marketing exuberance. It is _closer to**panic**_ , and it explains the AI industry's behavior far better than any amount of "innovation" talk does.
And the only story that justified spending that kind of money in the first place is one where AI eventually replaces enough expensive human labor to make that math work -- not augments it. **Replaces** it.
Which brings us to this week's news: Oracle just disclosed, in a federal regulatory filing, that it cut 21,000 jobs -- about 13 percent of its entire global workforce -- over the past year, while spending more than $55 billion on AI infrastructure, and named "the adoption and deployment of AI technologies" as a driver of the cuts. It's not alone. AI has now been the single most-cited reason for layoffs across American industries for three months running, with nearly 39,000 AI-attributed job losses in May alone. Meta cut 8,000 jobs that same month -- about 10 percent of its workforce -- to help fund its own AI buildout.
But here's the contradiction nobody in the industry wants to sit with out loud: ask the people actually using these tools every day -- in offices, hospitals, law firms, classrooms -- and they'll tell you something different than what the balance sheets need to be true.
AI is genuinely good at killing busywork. It drafts, it summarizes, it triages, it accelerates research. What it is not yet doing, outside a handful of administrative and entry-level functions, is replacing whole categories of skilled human judgment at the scale the debt requires.
Wall Street needs **replacement**. Most workplaces are still getting **augmentation**. That gap is the whole problem.
* * *
## Heads They Win. Tails You Lose.
Here is what almost nobody running these companies will say in public, but it is the truest sentence in this piece: **they are terrified.**
Not "cautious." Not "managing risk." **Terrified** , in the specific way that comes from building the single most leveraged bet in modern financial history and discovering there is no good outcome left on the table -- only a less-bad one.
**They have wedged themselves into the pivot point of an overleveraged spear that runs straight through the American economy, and very likely a measurable slice of the global one.** Every direction out of that position costs somebody something enormous.
So here is the trap, stated plainly, because I think it deserves to be said out loud:
**If AI does what the financing requires** -- if it guts payrolls deeply enough, fast enough, across enough of the economy to generate the cash flow that justifies $5.5 trillion in infrastructure -- _that is a five-alarm political and social crisis_. Fewer entry-level jobs. Fewer paths into a career. Flatter wages. A generation locked out of the ladder before they ever got a hand on it. We don't need 90% unemployment for this to be devastating. Half of that would be more than enough.
**If AI doesn 't do that** -- if it keeps being what it actually is right now, a powerful but limited productivity tool -- the bet doesn't pay off, and that is _also_ a crisis. Stock valuations built on AI-scale growth correct hard. Credit tightens for every company that financed its data centers with debt instead of cash. Refinancing gets expensive or disappears. Layoffs spread outward -- not just at AI labs, but across cloud providers, construction firms, utilities, suppliers, and every contractor who built capacity assuming the boom would keep going. Your 401(k) takes the hit whether or not you've ever opened a chatbot.
Both paths run straight through the same people. That is not a coincidence. That is the structure.
Look at what success requires next to what failure guarantees.
**Success** means proving, on a timeline of years rather than generations, that AI can do to the American labor market what no technology in history has managed that fast -- and it means the rest of us are left absorbing the social and political wreckage of that disruption while it happens.
**Failure** means the "Magnificent 7" default on trillions of dollars of debt that runs through bond funds, pension funds, insurance reserves, and bank balance sheets on at least two continents. _This is an unwind that won 't stay contained to "tech stocks" any more than subprime mortgages stayed contained to "the housing market" in 2008._
There is a real argument this could land worse than 2008, for one specific reason: in 2008, the toxic asset at the center of the storm was mortgages on houses people actually lived in, tied to a market regulators at least understood. This time, the asset at the center is chips, warehouses, and a labor-replacement story that has not been proven to work at the scale the money assumes it will.
If they succeed, it costs the country an economy that no longer needs most of us the way it used to. If they fail, it costs the country a financial crisis built on top of an economy that was already pretending it wasn't in the middle of one.
Either way, some CEO's disgrace doesn't make anybody's pension whole again.
Nobody currently running the AI industry knows for certain which outcome they're going to get. **All they know is that they are existentially required to destroy our economy in order to pay back their investors.**
That is the most honest thing I can tell you about where we actually stand.
* * *
## Who Profits, Who Pays
Here's the part that turns this from an economics story into a moral one.
If the bet pays off, the executives, founders, and early investors cash out on the way up -- stock sales, buybacks, golden exits -- long before the social cost of mass displacement lands on anyone else's desk. If the bet fails, the people holding index funds, pensions, and 401(k)s eat the correction, because that's who's exposed, whether they consented to the exposure or not.
**Either way, the people who steal the wealth are not the people who absorb the hit.**
And if you're wondering what a country does to manage the social fallout of an economy that's quietly engineering its way toward needing fewer of us -- watch where the money is already going. Surveillance contracts. "Public safety" AI tools sold to police departments and federal agencies.
And **private detention capacity** that the two largest prison contractors say is generating record profits -- one of them posted a nearly 700 percent jump in annual profit last year alone -- while their own investors complain, on earnings calls, that the government isn't filling beds fast enough to satisfy them.*
Nobody has to announce a plan for managing the human fallout of an economy that needs fewer people. You can just watch what's being built, and ask yourself why.
* * *
## What We Actually Need
I don't think the answer is to reject the technology. For one thing, that means ceding real human amplification capabilities to the billionaires and predators among us, and that's not OK with me. For another: _useful_ and _overpriced_ aren't opposites -- they were both true of railroads, and the internet, and fiber optic cable before this.
The lesson from every one of those bubbles is the same: the technology survived. The real question was always **who got rich, who got protected on the hard way down from "hype bubble" to "plateau of usefulness," **and**who got left holding the bag.**
What we actually need is people in office who can read a systemic imbalance as fluently as they read the Constitution -- who ask who's exposed and who's protected before the bill comes due, not in the press conference afterward explaining why nobody saw it coming.
We need real transparency around AI-related debt and circular financing. We need pension protections that don't assume index funds are automatically safe just because they're diversified on paper.
We need wage insurance, portable benefits, and retraining that's funded before the layoffs hit, not announced after.
And we need regulators willing to ask hard questions about deals where the lender, the customer, and the supplier all turn out to be the same handful of companies.
Mostly, we need people willing to say the quiet part out loud: an industry asking us to reorganize the labor market, the power grid, and the retirement security of working people around a technology whose promised returns are still unproven at scale is not innovation policy. **It 's a leveraged bet placed with the other people's money, and America's future.**
You didn't get a vote on the bet. You can still get a vote on whether anyone answers for it.
* * *

clean_body: The AI industry bet trillions of dollars on replacing your job. If they're right, that's a crisis. If they're wrong, that's also a crisis. Either way, you're the one left holding the bag. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more ? The AI industry bet trillions of dollars on replacing your job. If they're right, that's a crisis. If they're wrong, that's also a crisis. Either way, you're the one left holding the bag. | | | Jun 30 | | | | | | | | | | | | A quick note before we start: this piece is about the civilian AI economy -- the financial structure behind chatbots, cloud computing, and the trillions of dollars chasing all of it. I have a separate, much harder piece coming on the military applications of AI, and that one does not give any benefit of the doubt. This one is about your job, your pension, and your power bill. In 2024, a Swedish fintech company called Klarna built an AI customer-service assistant with OpenAI for somewhere around $2 to $3 million. In its first month alone, it handled work equivalent to roughly 700 full-time agents. Klarna projected the assistant would add about $40 million to company profit that year. Run the ratio: $40 million in value, generated by avoiding the need for about 700 workers, off a $2-to-$3-million build. That's the spreadsheet every CFO in the country is staring at right now. If AI deployment works like that, it pays for itself dozens of times over in a single year. That spreadsheet is the reason Nvidia is now worth more than $5 trillion. It's the reason seven tech stocks make up roughly a third of the entire S&P 500. It's the reason your pension fund, your 401(k), your state retirement system quietly became a leveraged bet on whether artificial intelligence delivers on promises it hasn't fully kept yet -- promises that would gut the economy as we've known it. And nobody asked you. Nobody asked you when Nvidia became worth more than any other company on Earth. Nobody asked you when your retirement savings became collateral for a bet you never consented to. Nobody asked you when the people selling you the future started needing you to believe in it more than they needed the technology to actually work. You didn't get a vote. You got a balance statement. And if some part of you has felt, these past couple of years, like something about the AI story doesn't quite add up -- like the hype is a half-step ahead of the actual product, like the people selling you the future have a few too many reasons to need you to believe them -- trust that feeling. You're not behind. You're paying attention. Here's what's actually going on. | | ---|---|--- The Story We're Being Sold The pitch is simple: artificial intelligence is the next industrial revolution. It will supercharge productivity, write your code, draft your emails, and eventually run a meaningful share of the economy with less human labor than we've ever needed before. Some of that is real. I use AI tools myself, for research, and they're genuinely useful -- they kill busywork, they help me think through strategy, they help me make the most of every minute of time. This isn't an anti-technology piece. But "useful" and "worth what Wall Street has bet on it" are two different questions. The gap between them is where the danger lives. Follow the Money As of this week, Nvidia is worth more than $5 trillion. Microsoft is sitting around $2.7 trillion. Oracle, even after a rough June, is still worth roughly half a trillion. Add in Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Tesla, and those seven companies -- the "Magnificent Seven" -- make up roughly a third of the entire S&P 500. That matters because, unless you've found some way to opt out of American capitalism's only real retirement system, you almost certainly own a slice of all of them. Index funds. Target-date funds. The teachers' pension. The firefighters' fund. The state employees' retirement system. They all hold the S&P 500 heavily, as what's assumed to be a safe, diversified, averaged holding that doesn't rely on any individual industry... -- but the S&P 500 is now, by design, a concentrated bet on a handful of AI companies , whether you chose that exposure or not. According to a Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis analysis, AI-related investment -- chips, software, data centers, research and development -- accounted for roughly 39% of all U.S. economic growth in the first three quarters of 2025. Strip that spending out, and the "strong economy" DC keeps congratulating itself on mostly disappears. We are not in an AI-adjacent economy. We are in an AI-dependent one. And here's the part that should make us nervous: behind all those trillions in market cap is a question nobody in power wants to answer: How much of that "demand" is real customers buying a real product, and how much of it is a handful of companies financing each other in a loop? The Circular Economy Machine In March, OpenAI closed a $122 billion funding round at a valuation north of $850 billion. The headline made it sound like a wall of investor cash. Look closer and the structure tells a different story. Nvidia's $30 billion of that round is largely compute credits, not cash -- money that flows back to Nvidia as OpenAI buys Nvidia's chips. Amazon put in $50 billion, but $35 billion of it is contingent on OpenAI either going public or hitting an artificial-general-intelligence milestone by year's end, meaning the actual committed cash on day one was a fraction of the headline number. SoftBank's $30 billion arrives in quarterly installments tied to OpenAI hitting its own targets along the way. Meanwhile, Oracle has taken on a roughly $300 billion contractual obligation to supply OpenAI with computing capacity through 2032 -- financed through aggressive borrowing, against a balance sheet that just posted negative free cash flow of nearly $24 billion. Nvidia invests in OpenAI. OpenAI spends that money on Nvidia chips and Oracle compute. Oracle borrows billions to build the data centers OpenAI needs, betting OpenAI's future revenue covers the debt. Around and around it goes. None of this is illegal. None of it is necessarily fraud in the technical sense -- whether it's fraud in the moral sense, or monopoly, or simply an absolutely terrible idea, is a different question. When the chipmaker is also the investor, and the customer is also the landlord, and the financing itself is generating the "demand" rather than the other way around, you have to ask how much of this economy would still exist if the money stopped flowing. Now return to that Klarna spreadsheet, because it explains everything that comes next. What "Replacing One Job" Is Actually Worth Here's a question worth answering plainly: is there an actual ratio connecting "one job gone" to "one dollar in AI revenue"? Nobody publishes an official industry-wide formula. But there is a real mechanism underneath it, and it isn't complicated once you see it laid bare. A company buys an AI tool for one reason: because the tool costs less than the human labor it lets the company avoid hiring or stop paying for. That's the entire business case, underneath a hundred different slide decks. Klarna's math was clean on day one. But by 2025, Klarna was quietly rehiring humans, because the AI couldn't reliably handle complex disputes, fraud claims, or anything requiring real judgment -- the harder, messier third of the actual job. The ratio that looked so beautiful on the spreadsheet fell apart the moment the work got complicated. That's the entire AI economy, in miniature. Multiply Klarna's story across every customer-service floor, every law firm, every hospital back office, every accounting department in America, and you get the real shape of the problem: the ratio works beautifully on the routine, repetitive slice of almost any job, and breaks down on the skilled, judgment-heavy slice that's usually most of what the job actually is. Every dollar of revenue flowing to Nvidia, Microsoft, and Oracle ultimately depends on enough companies finding that math attractive across enough of the workforce to add up to trillions of dollars in sustained spending. So far, the receipts say it adds up on the easy third. The debt was priced as if it adds up on the whole job. The Catch-22 Now here's where it gets fatal. JPMorgan currently projects $5.5 trillion in global AI infrastructure spending by 2030, with roughly $4.1 trillion of it financed through debt, not cash. More than $300 billion in AI and data-center bonds have already been issued in 2026 alone. Let's take a moment to get exquisitely clear about what "the debt has to be serviced" actually means, because this is the piece that explains everything else in this story. When a company borrows money by selling a bond, it owes two separate things. The principal is the original amount borrowed. The interest is rent, charged every single year, just for the privilege of having borrowed the money at all. You can pay only the interest for years and never touch the principal -- the same way you can pay the minimum on a credit card forever without the balance ever shrinking. But skip an interest payment, even once, and you 're in default. The lender doesn't care how brilliant your business plan is. They want their check, in full, on the date printed on the bond. Now scale that up to AI-industry size. Some of the roughly $4.1 trillion in projected debt is high-grade, pricing somewhere around 5 to 6 percent interest. A growing share is riskier, junk-rated data-center debt, which has been pricing at 7 to 9 percent, with at least one widely reported deal carrying a 12.5 percent coupon. Even using a conservative blended estimate of 6 to 8 percent, the interest alone on $4.1 trillion comes out to somewhere between roughly $245 billion and $330 billion. Every single year. For as long as that debt is outstanding -- before a single dollar of the original $4.1 trillion gets paid back. Sit with that number. Two hundred and forty-five to three hundred and thirty billion dollars, every year, just to stay current on interest -- more than the entire annual economic output of most countries on the planet, and that's before the principal is touched at all. That money has to come from somewhere real: customers paying for AI products at a scale that generates that much actual cash flow, growing every year fast enough to keep pace as more debt gets issued. And the only proven way AI generates that kind of return right now -- per the Klarna math above -- is by displacing labor costs at scale. Not gently assisting. Displacing. If that doesn't scale fast enough across enough of the economy, the cash flow doesn't show up... -- and the interest payment is still due on the date printed on the bond, regardless of how the technology is actually performing in the real world that quarter. This is the fundamental, desperate engine behind the hype. It is not marketing exuberance. It is closer topanic , and it explains the AI industry's behavior far better than any amount of "innovation" talk does. And the only story that justified spending that kind of money in the first place is one where AI eventually replaces enough expensive human labor to make that math work -- not augments it. Replaces it. Which brings us to this week's news: Oracle just disclosed, in a federal regulatory filing, that it cut 21,000 jobs -- about 13 percent of its entire global workforce -- over the past year, while spending more than $55 billion on AI infrastructure, and named "the adoption and deployment of AI technologies" as a driver of the cuts. It's not alone. AI has now been the single most-cited reason for layoffs across American industries for three months running, with nearly 39,000 AI-attributed job losses in May alone. Meta cut 8,000 jobs that same month -- about 10 percent of its workforce -- to help fund its own AI buildout. But here's the contradiction nobody in the industry wants to sit with out loud: ask the people actually using these tools every day -- in offices, hospitals, law firms, classrooms -- and they'll tell you something different than what the balance sheets need to be true. AI is genuinely good at killing busywork. It drafts, it summarizes, it triages, it accelerates research. What it is not yet doing, outside a handful of administrative and entry-level functions, is replacing whole categories of skilled human judgment at the scale the debt requires. Wall Street needs replacement. Most workplaces are still getting augmentation. That gap is the whole problem. Heads They Win. Tails You Lose. Here is what almost nobody running these companies will say in public, but it is the truest sentence in this piece: they are terrified. Not "cautious." Not "managing risk." Terrified , in the specific way that comes from building the single most leveraged bet in modern financial history and discovering there is no good outcome left on the table -- only a less-bad one. They have wedged themselves into the pivot point of an overleveraged spear that runs straight through the American economy, and very likely a measurable slice of the global one. Every direction out of that position costs somebody something enormous. So here is the trap, stated plainly, because I think it deserves to be said out loud: If AI does what the financing requires -- if it guts payrolls deeply enough, fast enough, across enough of the economy to generate the cash flow that justifies $5.5 trillion in infrastructure -- that is a five-alarm political and social crisis. Fewer entry-level jobs. Fewer paths into a career. Flatter wages. A generation locked out of the ladder before they ever got a hand on it. We don't need 90% unemployment for this to be devastating. Half of that would be more than enough. If AI doesn 't do that -- if it keeps being what it actually is right now, a powerful but limited productivity tool -- the bet doesn't pay off, and that is also a crisis. Stock valuations built on AI-scale growth correct hard. Credit tightens for every company that financed its data centers with debt instead of cash. Refinancing gets expensive or disappears. Layoffs spread outward -- not just at AI labs, but across cloud providers, construction firms, utilities, suppliers, and every contractor who built capacity assuming the boom would keep going. Your 401(k) takes the hit whether or not you've ever opened a chatbot. Both paths run straight through the same people. That is not a coincidence. That is the structure. Look at what success requires next to what failure guarantees. Success means proving, on a timeline of years rather than generations, that AI can do to the American labor market what no technology in history has managed that fast -- and it means the rest of us are left absorbing the social and political wreckage of that disruption while it happens. Failure means the "Magnificent 7" default on trillions of dollars of debt that runs through bond funds, pension funds, insurance reserves, and bank balance sheets on at least two continents. This is an unwind that won 't stay contained to "tech stocks" any more than subprime mortgages stayed contained to "the housing market" in 2008. There is a real argument this could land worse than 2008, for one specific reason: in 2008, the toxic asset at the center of the storm was mortgages on houses people actually lived in, tied to a market regulators at least understood. This time, the asset at the center is chips, warehouses, and a labor-replacement story that has not been proven to work at the scale the money assumes it will. If they succeed, it costs the country an economy that no longer needs most of us the way it used to. If they fail, it costs the country a financial crisis built on top of an economy that was already pretending it wasn't in the middle of one. Either way, some CEO's disgrace doesn't make anybody's pension whole again. Nobody currently running the AI industry knows for certain which outcome they're going to get. All they know is that they are existentially required to destroy our economy in order to pay back their investors. That is the most honest thing I can tell you about where we actually stand. Who Profits, Who Pays Here's the part that turns this from an economics story into a moral one. If the bet pays off, the executives, founders, and early investors cash out on the way up -- stock sales, buybacks, golden exits -- long before the social cost of mass displacement lands on anyone else's desk. If the bet fails, the people holding index funds, pensions, and 401(k)s eat the correction, because that's who's exposed, whether they consented to the exposure or not. Either way, the people who steal the wealth are not the people who absorb the hit. And if you're wondering what a country does to manage the social fallout of an economy that's quietly engineering its way toward needing fewer of us -- watch where the money is already going. Surveillance contracts. "Public safety" AI tools sold to police departments and federal agencies. And private detention capacity that the two largest prison contractors say is generating record profits -- one of them posted a nearly 700 percent jump in annual profit last year alone -- while their own investors complain, on earnings calls, that the government isn't filling beds fast enough to satisfy them. Nobody has to announce a plan for managing the human fallout of an economy that needs fewer people. You can just watch what's being built, and ask yourself why. What We Actually Need I don't think the answer is to reject the technology. For one thing, that means ceding real human amplification capabilities to the billionaires and predators among us, and that's not OK with me. For another: useful and overpriced aren't opposites -- they were both true of railroads, and the internet, and fiber optic cable before this. The lesson from every one of those bubbles is the same: the technology survived. The real question was always who got rich, who got protected on the hard way down from "hype bubble" to "plateau of usefulness," andwho got left holding the bag. What we actually need is people in office who can read a systemic imbalance as fluently as they read the Constitution -- who ask who's exposed and who's protected before the bill comes due, not in the press conference afterward explaining why nobody saw it coming. We need real transparency around AI-related debt and circular financing. We need pension protections that don't assume index funds are automatically safe just because they're diversified on paper. We need wage insurance, portable benefits, and retraining that's funded before the layoffs hit, not announced after. And we need regulators willing to ask hard questions about deals where the lender, the customer, and the supplier all turn out to be the same handful of companies. Mostly, we need people willing to say the quiet part out loud: an industry asking us to reorganize the labor market, the power grid, and the retirement security of working people around a technology whose promised returns are still unproven at scale is not innovation policy. It 's a leveraged bet placed with the other people's money, and America's future. You didn't get a vote on the bet. You can still get a vote on whether anyone answers for it. Care. Courage. The Constitution. If this is the kind of thing you want explained before it 's too late to matter instead of after, subscribe. I'll keep doing the homework. name: Dan Ahlers
subject: Peter, here's where I've been.
disclaimer_text: PAID FOR BY DAN AHLERS FOR GOVERNOR
body:
|
---
| |
---
| | | |
---
| |
---
| | | [DONATE](https://us.list-manage.com/GKkCCswIZAS?e=cee7b49c04&c2id=3adc23449cf80dcda430cceaf3c4b05d)

| |
---
| | | [VOLUNTEER](https://us.list-manage.com/AJOlnpenOS_?e=cee7b49c04&c2id=3adc23449cf80dcda430cceaf3c4b05d)
---
| |
---

| | | | | |
---
Canistota Dairy Farm Visit

I'm grateful for the opportunity to hear directly from the people who are the backbone of South Dakota's economy, our farmers, ranchers, and agricultural leaders.

One issue that came up repeatedly was the inconsistency between state and federal regulations. When agencies provide conflicting guidance or no guidance at all. It creates unnecessary uncertainty for producers who are simply trying to run their operations, make sound business decisions, and provide for their families. Our farmers deserve clarity, consistency, and a government that works with them instead of creating additional obstacles.

Good leadership begins with listening, but it doesn't end there. For too long, many farmers have felt that their concerns were heard but not acted upon. My commitment is to ensure agriculture has a meaningful seat at the table when important decisions are made. By listening, collaborating, and bringing producers into the policymaking process, we can develop practical solutions that strengthen agriculture and rural communities across South Dakota.

| | | | |
---
78th Annual Czech Days

It was a pleasure to celebrate 155 years of Tabor, South Dakota, and to honor the rich and meaningful history of the early founders of this small but mighty community. Tabor is a reminder that South Dakota’s story is not only written in our largest cities, but in the small towns that have carried our values, traditions, and way of life across generations.

Communities like Tabor exist all across our state, each with its own unique history and identity, yet all contributing to the larger fabric of what makes South Dakota special. These towns are built on hard work, faith, family, and a deep sense of place. When we support community events like Czech Days, we are doing more than celebrating a festival, we are investing in the people and traditions that keep these communities strong and connected.

Preserving and celebrating these traditions is essential not only for honoring our past, but for inspiring future generations to stay, build their lives, and continue the legacy of South Dakota’s small towns. When our communities thrive, the entire state is stronger for it.

| | | |
---
| |
---
Davis Meet and Greet

It was a pleasure to spend time in Davis, South Dakota, and connect with residents about the issues that matter most to their community and to rural South Dakota more broadly. These conversations are always valuable, offering insight into the everyday challenges and opportunities facing small towns across our state.

I am especially grateful to the Merrill and Olsen families for their hospitality and for hosting this event. Their willingness to open their home and bring neighbors together reflects the strength of small-town South Dakota and creates meaningful opportunities to listen, learn, and engage directly with the people we serve.

| | |
---
| |
---
Desserts with Democrats

After 24 hours of traveling across the state, the day ended on a sweet note. At Kuehn Park in Sioux Falls, I enjoyed homemade desserts and, more importantly, homegrown perspectives about what people in our largest city are experiencing and what they want and need from their state government.

The conversations covered a wide range of issues, from the rising cost of housing and property taxes to concerns about healthcare access, education, and the strength of our workforce. What stood out most was the shared desire for practical solutions and a government that listens and responds with common sense and accountability.

POLICY PERSPECTIVES

| |
---
Here’s the latest from across the campaign trail—key updates, major milestones, and where we’re headed next.

| | | |
---
| |
---
Supporting Farmers

Supporting our farmers starts with listening to them and prioritizing their presence at critical decision making moments. South Dakota agriculture has always been the backbone of our economy, but we cannot rely on doing things the same way we did in the past and expect different results. We need to diversify the crops and products we produce while expanding new markets for South Dakota farmers and ranchers. That means investing in homegrown entrepreneurs who want to create value-added opportunities here instead of watching those jobs leave the state.

| | | [READ THE FULL ARTICLE HERE](https://us.list-manage.com/11s_Aq4kC1i?e=cee7b49c04&c2id=3adc23449cf80dcda430cceaf3c4b05d)
---
| |
---
What’s Next.

I will be walking in a number of Fourth of July parades including Deadwood, Lead, Rapid City, Belle Fourche, and Spearfish. I look forward to celebrating our country with South Dakotan communities. If you’re in the area and are interested in marching in a parade with me, you can RSVP with the volunteer button at the top of this email.

With your help, we can win.

Be a part of my grassroots campaign today.

Every legitimate government on the planet reserves one decision to itself above all others: who gets to be a citizen. This supreme sovereign authority has been the hallmark of all legitimate regimes since even before the Roman Republic.
You can argue about tariffs, about borders, about who gets a visa and who gets turned away at the gate. But the question of citizenship itself -- who is one of us -- is the bedrock sovereign act. It is the one thing a nation does not let strangers decide for it.
As of this morning, the United States is the exception. The United States has now granted authority to decide who is a U.S. citizen to any non-American who intentionally violates our borders -- our sovereignty -- whether in desperation or as part of a long-term anti-American stratagem.
Chief Justice John Roberts joined the three female leftists on the Supreme Court in ruling that the U.S. Constitution precludes the U.S. government from deciding who is and is not a U.S. citizen.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..AeXR5hDJHscpLBDb5G1_6bOEZgeciODNtfg32eFRZBY?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=204344395)
In _Trump v. Barbara_ , decided Tuesday, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that President Donald Trump's executive order on birthright citizenship is unconstitutional. The holding is blunt: "Children born in the United States to parents unlawfully or temporarily present are 'subject to the jurisdiction' of the United States and are citizens at birth under the Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship Clause." Chief Justice Roberts wrote for the majority. "We keep that promise today," he concluded.
In other words, a Chinese tourist who flies to America eight months pregnant for the express purpose of dropping a U.S. citizen anchor baby now has the constitutional stamp of approval. Thanks, John. Ditto for the Central American illegal alien who steps one foot onto American soil before giving birth.
In tracing the English common-law roots of birthright citizenship, Roberts wrote that "a foreign mother could enter the British Isles, give birth, and leave with her child the very next day, and that child would remain a British subject." The child, he explained, owed allegiance to the sovereign who protected him at birth, "no matter how 'momentary and uncertain' his presence." A sovereign's jurisdiction, the Court held, makes "no exception for those only temporarily present within the sovereign's territory."
According to Roberts, a foreign national who arrives, gives birth, departs with a new citizen in tow, and then later benefits from the citizenship status of the child is not exploiting a loophole or an ambiguity in American law but is exercising a constitutional right precisely as it was designed. Show up, deliver, leave. The baby is an American, and there is nothing the American people or their elected representatives can do about it.
Because Roberts determined that the U.S. Constitution itself enshrines the right of any woman on the planet to drop an anchor baby in America, it would require a constitutional amendment, not merely a congressional bill, to fix this egregious attack on American sovereignty.
The dissenters saw exactly where this leads.
Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Gorsuch, did not mince words: "The Court today takes the extraordinary step of holding facially unconstitutional the President's Order excluding from citizenship the children of foreign temporary visitors and illegal aliens." The majority's account of citizenship history, Thomas wrote, "is not historically accurate." His reading turns on a word the majority worked hard to bury -- domicile. To Thomas, the Fourteenth Amendment was written for people who had nowhere else to go, the freed slaves who called America home and were owed full membership in the only nation they had. It was not drafted as a turnstile for the children of people passing through on a tourist visa -- to say nothing of Chinese Communist hostiles exploiting birthright citizenship for long-term geopolitical reasons.
Justice Alito, in a separate dissent, was equally direct: "The Court has made a serious mistake." He pointed out what the majority preferred not to dwell on, i.e., that this reading makes America a global outlier. Other than Canada, Alito noted, the United States now stands essentially alone among affluent nations in handing automatic, unconditional citizenship to the children of temporary visitors. The wealthy democracies we like to compare ourselves to looked at this rule and declined to adopt it. We have now constitutionalized it. It will be permanent until the end it now hastens.
The Chief Justice's answer to all of this, offered at oral argument back in April, was that birth tourism simply wasn't a problem anyone imagined in 1868. "It's a new world," he conceded, but "it's the same Constitution." It is a tidy line. It is also an excuse, and a confession. The Court has frozen 1868 in amber and ruled that a world the Framers could never have anticipated must be governed as though that world still exists.
The Chief Justice's bizarre conduct, stretching back even to his obtuse ruling on the Affordable Care Act, makes you wonder what kind of frazzledrip blackmail they've got on Roberts that's turned him into a saggier version of the pink-haired liberals wagging Palestinian flags in the streets.
I have spent the better part of two years documenting what Chinese transnational networks actually do when they discover a seam in American law. In rural Maine, it was the cannabis grows. The lesson of that work is simple, and it does not flatter us: where America leaves a legal structure unguarded, organized actors will industrialize their use of it. Not abuse it occasionally. Industrialize it.
Birth tourism is that same playbook, run at the maternity ward.
Investigative reporter Peter Schweizer, president of the Government Accountability Institute, laid this out under oath before Congress this spring. He described an "industrial" operation. "In China alone, we have identified more than 1,000 birth tourism companies that are almost exclusively focused on the United States," he testified. These are not back-alley arrangements. They are concierge services. Roughly $100,000 buys travel, lodging, medical care, and a legal team to walk the citizenship paperwork through after delivery. Schweizer, drawing on Chinese government estimates of tens of thousands of such births per year, told senators that somewhere between 750,000 and 1.5 million U.S. citizens may currently be growing up inside the People's Republic of China. Children who will reach voting age, can sponsor relatives for residency at 21, and in some cases trace directly to military officers, propaganda officials, and ranking members of the Chinese Communist Party. He titled his book on the broader phenomenon The Invisible Coup. The title is not subtle. Neither is the strategy it describes.
Chief Justice Roberts just endorsed that coup.

Hi Peter, you’ve probably heard over and over again that this election is the biggest, most important of our lifetime – and honestly, I agree. There’s so much at stake, from reproductive rights, access to health care, affordability, action on climate change, and more. Even our democracy is on the line!
But amid all the chaos and the pressure to get this election right, I know in my gut that we can do this – because Minnesotans are prepared.
I think about how when Trump sent ICE agents to flood our state, Minnesotans didn't flinch.
We showed up for one another. We protested peacefully in freezing temperatures, and our neighbors stood guard outside the schools. Volunteers delivered groceries to families who were rightfully afraid to leave their homes. Communities organized, showed up, and took care of each other, even when it was hard, even when it was scary.
I have never been more proud to be a Minnesotan – and I wholeheartedly believe that Minnesota’s response is the model for fighting back against Trump. You show up. You take care of each other. You don't back down.
And when we flip the House in November, it will be because of people like you staying engaged and showing up every single time. Because that's what this moment demands.
If you’re with me, I could really use your help before our FEC deadline tonight at midnight. A contribution of any amount helps us keep this fight going. [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/morrison-em-26]
You can contribute online right here: https://secure.actblue.com/donate/morrison-em-26 [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/morrison-em-26]
Together we can hold this seat, flip the House, and continue bringing Minnesota's spirit of courage and community into the halls of Congress for the fights ahead.
With gratitude and resolve,
Kelly

body:
It seems like every election is framed as the most important we've faced.
But with the attacks on our democracy and our fundamental right to vote, especially in the wake of the Supreme Court's decisions that dismantle the Voting Rights Act, the importance of the midterms cannot be understated .
We have no time to waste. Chip in $35 or more right now to defend our fundamental right to vote! >> [http://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-power?refcode=063026_4&amount=35]
Voter Action Project [https://voteractionproject.org/]
Team
The Constitution places the authority to run elections squarely with the states and Congress – NOT with the federal government.
But now, the President has issued another executive order imposing sweeping new federal control over election administration.
Make no mistake, Team, this is yet another unlawful attempt by this MAGA administration to sow confusion and distrust ahead of the fall midterm elections.
We're doing everything in our power to fight back and protect the right to vote , including:
➜ Registering eligible voters
➜ Putting election information directly in the hands of voters
➜ Combating election misinformation
➜ Advocating at every level to keep our elections truly free and fair
Team, it will take massive resources to stand up to this new executive order in time to make a difference before the midterm elections. We need your help ASAP: Will you chip in $35 or whatever you can afford right now? >> [http://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-power?refcode=063026_4&amount=35]
If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately:
GIVE $15 NOW ➜ [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-power?express_lane=true&refcode=063026_4&amount=15] GIVE $25 NOW ➜ [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-power?express_lane=true&refcode=063026_4&amount=25] GIVE $50 NOW ➜ [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-power?express_lane=true&refcode=063026_4&amount=50]

The executive order purports to address “non-citizen voting.”
States, however, already have proven systems in place to verify voter eligibility, non-citizen voting is already a federal crime, and instances are vanishingly rare.
Rather than solving a real problem, this order manufactures one to justify granting this administration unprecedented authority over a process which the Constitution clearly delegates to the states and to Congress.
It's simple: This executive order is dangerous, unlawful, and harmful to voters.
We will never stay silent when the right to vote is attacked, Team, including by a hostile administration in control of the federal government.
If you’re with us, please chip in $35 or whatever you can to fuel our work empowering voters ahead of the 2026 elections >> [http://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-power?refcode=063026_4&amount=35]
Voter Action Project [https://voteractionproject.org/]

Integrity First Voter Action Project is dedicated to expanding ballot access and increasing voter participation across the country.
Since the Supreme Court gutted key provisions in the Voting Rights Act, extreme politicians have taken advantage to pass harsh laws that restrict access to the ballot box. These restrictions particularly affect disadvantaged communities and people of color. It’s our goal to bring awareness to these laws wherever they may crop up and organize voters to take action to ensure the right to vote is available to everyone in their states and communities.
Your support is crucial to our efforts. Will you donate today to help us protect voting rights? [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/integrity-first-voter-action-project-1?refcode=063026_4&amount=20]
